title: Transcription and RNA Processing
summary: Follow how RNA polymerase reads genes and how the new RNA is processed into mature mRNA.

lessons.title: RNA Polymerases: Bacterial and Eukaryotic

levels.kid:
Your DNA is like a giant cookbook locked in a library. The recipes can't leave the library. So the cell makes a copy of one recipe at a time. The copy is called **RNA**.

The machine that makes the copy is called **RNA polymerase**. It slides along the DNA and reads it letter by letter. As it reads, it builds a matching RNA strand, like a copy machine that types as it goes.

Bacteria have just one kind of copy machine. Your cells have three main kinds. Each one copies different types of recipes.

Some mushrooms make a poison that jams one of these machines. That is why those mushrooms are so dangerous to eat.
levels.hs:
**Transcription** is the process of copying a gene's DNA sequence into RNA. The enzyme that does it is **RNA polymerase**.

RNA polymerase:
- Reads one DNA strand, called the **template strand**, and builds RNA that matches the other strand. In RNA, the base uracil (U) takes the place of thymine (T).
- Joins nucleotides in the **5' to 3' direction**, adding each new one to the growing end.
- Unlike DNA polymerase, it does not need a **primer**. It can start a new chain from scratch.

**Bacteria** such as *E. coli* use one RNA polymerase for all their genes. A helper protein called the **sigma factor** attaches to it and steers it to the start of genes.

**Eukaryotes** (plants, animals, fungi) split the work among three main nuclear polymerases:
- **Pol I** makes most ribosomal RNA (rRNA).
- **Pol II** makes messenger RNA (mRNA), which carries protein recipes.
- **Pol III** makes transfer RNA (tRNA) and other small RNAs.

A real example: the death cap mushroom (*Amanita phalloides*) contains **alpha-amanitin**, a toxin that blocks Pol II. Liver cells can no longer make new mRNA, so poisoning can cause liver failure. In bacteria, the tuberculosis antibiotic **rifampicin** works by blocking bacterial RNA polymerase, which is a different enzyme from ours.
levels.college:
All cellular RNA polymerases are multisubunit enzymes that make RNA from a DNA template. They need no primer and build the chain 5'→3' using ribonucleoside triphosphates (NTPs), releasing pyrophosphate.

**Bacterial RNA polymerase**
- The **core enzyme** has five subunits: α2ββ'ω. The large β and β' subunits form a crab-claw shape, with the active site between them. A catalytic **Mg2+** ion is held there by a conserved aspartate motif (NADFDGD) in β'.
- Adding a **σ factor** makes the **holoenzyme**, which can recognize promoters. **σ70** handles housekeeping genes. Other σ factors switch on whole groups of genes, such as σ32 for heat-shock genes or σ54 for nitrogen-related genes.
- **Rifampicin** binds β (encoded by *rpoB*) and blocks the path of the RNA once it is 2 to 3 nucleotides long. Mutations in *rpoB* cause most rifampicin resistance in *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*.

**Eukaryotic nuclear RNA polymerases**
- **Pol I** (14 subunits) works in the nucleolus and makes the 45S pre-rRNA, which is processed into 18S, 5.8S and 28S rRNA.
- **Pol II** (12 subunits) makes pre-mRNAs plus most snRNAs and miRNA precursors.
- **Pol III** (17 subunits) makes tRNAs, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA and 7SL RNA.
- The two largest subunits of each (in Pol II, RPB1 and RPB2) are related to bacterial β' and β. Five subunits are shared by all three enzymes.
- **α-amanitin** sensitivity separates them: Pol II is blocked at very low concentrations, Pol III at higher ones, and Pol I is resistant.

Pol II's largest subunit, RPB1, has a unique **C-terminal domain (CTD)**. It is made of repeats of the seven-amino-acid sequence YSPTSPS (52 in humans, 26 in yeast). Plants also have Pol IV and Pol V, which make RNAs used in gene silencing. Mitochondria use a single-subunit polymerase, POLRMT, related to the RNA polymerase of the T7 bacteriophage.
levels.phd:
Multisubunit RNA polymerases (msRNAPs) in bacteria, archaea and eukaryotes share a conserved catalytic core built around two **double-psi β-barrel** domains. Their last universal common ancestor almost certainly had one. Single-subunit polymerases (phage T7, POLRMT) belong instead to the polymerase I/pol A family and arose independently.

**Catalysis and dynamics.** The active site uses a two-metal-ion mechanism. Mg2+ A is held permanently by the NADFDGD motif. Mg2+ B arrives bound to the incoming NTP. Two mobile elements in β'/RPB1 drive each nucleotide-addition cycle:
- The **trigger loop** folds over a correctly paired NTP to close the active site.
- The **bridge helix** helps the enzyme move one base forward (translocation), probably by a Brownian ratchet.

Accuracy comes from selecting the right NTP plus **backtracking** and cleavage of misincorporated bases. Cleavage is stimulated by GreA/GreB in bacteria and **TFIIS** in eukaryotes. Error rates are about 10^-5 to 10^-6 per nucleotide. Inside the enzyme, roughly 12 to 14 bp of DNA stays unwound in the **transcription bubble**, with an RNA-DNA hybrid of about 8 to 9 bp.

**Inhibitor structural biology.** Bushnell, Cramer and Kornberg (2002) showed that α-amanitin binds near the bridge helix and trigger loop of Pol II. It traps the trigger loop and slows translocation by orders of magnitude, rather than blocking NTP binding. Rifampicin, by contrast, blocks the RNA exit path in bacterial β. Its binding pocket is absent from eukaryotic enzymes, which explains why it targets bacteria selectively.

**Specialization.** Pol I and Pol III have built-in subcomplexes that resemble general transcription factors. Pol I's A49/A34.5 resembles TFIIF/TFIIE. Pol I's A12.2 and Pol III's C11 carry a TFIIS-like cleavage domain. These features fit their dedicated, high-throughput roles. Pol I transcription of rDNA can account for up to about 60% of total transcription in rapidly growing yeast.

**The CTD.** Changing patterns of phosphorylation on Ser5, Ser2, Ser7, Thr4 and Tyr1 form a "CTD code." Ser5 is phosphorylated by CDK7 (TFIIH) and Ser2 by CDK9 (P-TEFb) and CDK12. Kornberg's structural work (Nobel Prize, 2006) and Roeder's identification of three polymerases by chromatography (1969) are classic studies. How literally the CTD code is "read" remains debated.
levels.expert:
Clinically and experimentally, RNA polymerase differences are exploited in three main ways: antimicrobial selectivity, toxicology, and engineered tools.

**Antimicrobials.** Rifamycins remain central to tuberculosis therapy. Resistance is the main problem. About 95% of rifampicin-resistant *M. tuberculosis* carries mutations in the 81-bp rifampicin-resistance-determining region (RRDR) of *rpoB*, most often S450L. The GeneXpert MTB/RIF assay detects RRDR mutations directly from sputum in under two hours. Pitfall: "disputed" low-level mutations (for example L430P) can test resistant on Xpert yet susceptible on standard phenotypic testing. **Fidaxomicin**, used for *Clostridioides difficile*, binds a different site, the β' switch region. This blocks closing of the clamp and gives no cross-resistance with rifamycins. Compensatory mutations in *rpoA*/*rpoC* restore fitness to resistant strains, which affects how far resistance spreads.

**Toxicology.** In amatoxin poisoning, OATP1B3 carries the toxin into hepatocytes, and it is recycled through enterohepatic circulation. Management focuses on interrupting this uptake and recycling. Silibinin, which blocks OATP uptake, is used, and liver transplant is reserved for fulminant failure. Antibody-drug conjugates using α-amanitin as a payload are now in trials. They exploit Pol II dependence, and loss of *POLR2A* alongside *TP53* in 17p-deleted cancers may increase sensitivity.

**Neurology and oncology links.** Pol III mutations (*POLR3A/B*) cause 4H hypomyelinating leukodystrophy. Mutations in *POLR1C/D* and in Pol I factors cause Treacher Collins syndrome. Pol I inhibition (CX-5461/pidnarulex, BMH-21) is being explored in cancers that depend heavily on ribosome biogenesis, such as MYC-driven tumors. CX-5461 also stabilizes G-quadruplexes, which makes its mechanism hard to attribute cleanly.

**Tools.** T7 RNA polymerase underpins in vitro transcription for mRNA vaccines. Its byproducts, especially double-stranded RNA, activate innate sensors and must be removed. Engineered T7 variants and better process control reduce them.

**Open questions** include how CTD condensates partition Pol II into transcriptional hubs, and whether Pol III's output can be selectively targeted in cancer.

keyPoints: RNA polymerase copies DNA into RNA 5'→3' without a primer
Bacteria use one core enzyme (α2ββ'ω) plus a σ factor to find promoters
Eukaryotes use Pol I (rRNA), Pol II (mRNA) and Pol III (tRNA, 5S rRNA)
Pol II's largest subunit has a repeated YSPTSPS C-terminal domain (CTD)
Rifampicin blocks bacterial RNA polymerase; α-amanitin blocks Pol II
All multisubunit RNA polymerases share an ancient conserved catalytic core

lessons.title: Promoters and General Transcription Factors

levels.kid:
Imagine a giant library where every book is a gene. A reader called **RNA polymerase** wants to copy one book. But how does it know where the story starts?

Each gene has a special sign just before its start, like a bus stop sign. This sign is called a **promoter**. It is made of DNA letters in a special order.

In our cells, the reader cannot find the sign alone. Helpers called **transcription factors** come first. One helper grabs the sign and bends the DNA, like folding a page corner. Then more helpers arrive, and finally the reader sits down in the right spot.

Once everyone is ready, the reader starts copying the gene into a message called RNA.
levels.hs:
Before a gene can be copied into RNA (**transcription**), the copying enzyme, **RNA polymerase**, has to find the right starting point. That starting region of DNA is the **promoter**, a stretch of DNA just upstream (before) the place where copying begins, called the **transcription start site**.

In bacteria, promoters have two short signature sequences: one about 10 base pairs before the start (TATAAT) and one about 35 base pairs before it (TTGACA). A protein called **sigma factor** attaches to RNA polymerase and lets it recognize these signals.

In eukaryotes like us, RNA polymerase II (which makes the RNAs that become messenger RNA) cannot recognize promoters by itself. It needs a team of proteins called **general transcription factors**, named TFIIA, TFIIB, TFIID, TFIIE, TFIIF and TFIIH. They assemble on the promoter in a rough order to form the **preinitiation complex**.

A famous promoter sequence is the **TATA box**, found about 25 to 30 base pairs upstream in many genes. A part of TFIID called **TATA-binding protein (TBP)** grips it and sharply bends the DNA, marking the spot.

Example: genes that must be switched on strongly and quickly in particular situations, like heat-shock genes, often have TATA boxes. Many "housekeeping" genes, which are on in nearly every cell, lack one and use other promoter elements instead.
levels.college:
A **promoter** is the cis-acting DNA region that positions RNA polymerase and sets the transcription start site (TSS, position +1). The **core promoter** spans roughly -40 to +40 and is distinct from proximal elements and distant enhancers.

**Bacteria.** The sigma70 holoenzyme recognizes the **-10 element (Pribnow box, TATAAT)** and the **-35 element (TTGACA)**, ideally spaced 17 bp apart. Some strong promoters (e.g., rRNA promoters) also have an AT-rich **UP element** contacted by the alpha subunit C-terminal domain. Alternative sigma factors (sigma32 for heat shock, sigma54 for nitrogen genes) recognize different promoter sequences, switching whole gene programs.

**Eukaryotic Pol II core promoter elements:**
- **TATA box** (TATAWAW, around -30): bound by TBP
- **BRE** (TFIIB recognition element) on either side of the TATA box
- **Inr** (initiator) spanning the TSS
- **DPE** (downstream promoter element, about +28 to +33) and **MTE**, bound by TAF subunits of TFIID

**Preinitiation complex (PIC) assembly**, classic stepwise model:
- **TFIID** (TBP plus about 13 TAFs) binds the promoter; TBP binds the minor groove and bends DNA by roughly 80 to 90 degrees
- **TFIIA** stabilizes TBP-DNA binding; **TFIIB** bridges TBP to Pol II and helps choose the TSS
- **Pol II-TFIIF** joins; then **TFIIE** recruits **TFIIH**
- TFIIH's **XPB** subunit (an ATP-dependent translocase) opens the DNA, and its **CDK7** kinase phosphorylates Ser5 of the Pol II CTD heptad repeats (YSPTSPS)

Only a minority of human promoters contain a TATA box. Most housekeeping genes use **CpG island** promoters with dispersed TSSs. TBP also works with Pol I (in SL1) and Pol III (in TFIIIB), which makes it a universal factor.
levels.phd:
Core promoter architecture predicts initiation behavior. Genome-wide TSS mapping (CAGE, from the FANTOM consortium) revealed two broad classes. **Focused promoters** have a single dominant TSS, often a TATA box or Inr, and are typical of tissue-specific and inducible genes. **Dispersed promoters** fire from many TSSs spread over 50 to 100 bp. They are typically CpG islands, which lack TATA boxes, carry H3K4me3, and sit in a nucleosome-depleted region (NDR) flanked by a well-positioned +1 nucleosome.

Structurally, TBP is a saddle-shaped protein whose concave underside binds the TATA minor groove. Two phenylalanine pairs intercalate between base steps and kink the DNA (Kim, Burley and Sigler, 1993). TATA-less promoters still need TBP. Here TFIID's TAFs make the sequence contacts: TAF1/TAF2 bind Inr and TAF6/TAF9 bind DPE. Cryo-EM work by the Nogales lab showed that TFIID shifts between lobe conformations during promoter engagement and loads TBP onto DNA in a defined orientation.

The stepwise assembly model came from Roeder's in vitro reconstitution. It has been challenged by the **holoenzyme** model, in which Pol II arrives preassembled with Mediator and some GTFs. Single-molecule imaging (e.g., in yeast extracts) shows fast, partially ordered assembly with many failed attempts. Both views are partly true.

TSS selection differs between species. In mammals, initiation occurs about 30 bp downstream of TATA. In *S. cerevisiae*, the PIC scans 40 to 120 bp downstream, driven by TFIIH translocase activity and guided by the TFIIB B-reader. **Mediator**, a roughly 26-subunit complex, transmits activator signals to the PIC and stimulates CDK7. CDK7 phosphorylation of Ser5 (and Ser7) helps promoter escape. TFIIH's helicase XPD is dispensable for transcription but essential in nucleotide excision repair, a dual role that links the two processes.

There are controversies. One is whether TFIID is universally required, since in yeast SAGA also delivers TBP to most genes (Warfield et al., 2017). Another is how much intrinsic core promoter sequence, rather than enhancers, sets expression level and responsiveness.
levels.expert:
Promoter biology now links mechanism to disease and therapy in several concrete ways.

**TFIIH as a clinical intersection.** Mutations in XPB (ERCC3) and XPD (ERCC2) cause xeroderma pigmentosum, trichothiodystrophy and Cockayne overlap syndromes. In trichothiodystrophy, the brittle hair and neurodevelopmental features are thought to come partly from reduced TFIIH stability, which lowers transcription in highly transcribing differentiating cells, and not only from repair defects. **Triptolide**, a natural product, covalently binds XPB and blocks its ATPase. It globally suppresses Pol II initiation and has been explored (as the prodrug minnelide) in pancreatic cancer.

**CDK7 inhibitors.** THZ1 (covalent) and selective agents such as samuraciclib target CDK7. Tumors driven by super-enhancer-dependent oncogenes (MYCN neuroblastoma, some triple-negative breast cancers) are disproportionately sensitive, a phenomenon called "transcriptional addiction." The pitfall is that CDK7 is also the CDK-activating kinase for cell-cycle CDKs, which makes on-target effects hard to separate.

**Promoter mutations in cancer.** Recurrent *TERT* promoter mutations (C228T, C250T) create de novo ETS/GABP binding sites. They are strikingly common in glioblastoma and in *IDH*-wild-type gliomas and are now part of WHO CNS5 diagnostic criteria. A neurosurgery-relevant example: an *IDH*-wildtype diffuse astrocytoma with a *TERT* promoter mutation is classified as molecular glioblastoma, grade 4, even without necrosis on histology.

**Engineering and gene therapy.** Viral vector cargo limits favor compact promoters. Strong ubiquitous promoters (CMV, CAG) can silence over time through CpG methylation. Neuron-specific choices (hSyn, CaMKIIa) trade strength for specificity. Massively parallel reporter assays now test thousands of synthetic core promoters, showing that element combinations and spacing matter more than any single motif.

**Research pitfalls.** CAGE- or PRO-cap-defined TSSs often disagree with annotated gene starts. Many promoters are bidirectional, producing upstream antisense transcripts, so "promoter" calls from peak data need strand-aware interpretation.

**Open questions.** Why are TBP paralogs (TRF2, TBPL2) used in germ cells? And how is PIC assembly kinetically coupled to transcriptional bursting seen in live-cell imaging?

keyPoints: A promoter is the DNA region that positions RNA polymerase at the transcription start site
Bacterial sigma70 recognizes the -10 (TATAAT) and -35 (TTGACA) elements
Eukaryotic Pol II needs general transcription factors: TFIIA, B, D, E, F and H
TBP within TFIID binds the TATA box and sharply bends DNA
TFIIH opens DNA (XPB) and phosphorylates Pol II CTD Ser5 (CDK7)
Most human promoters lack TATA and are CpG islands with dispersed start sites

lessons.title: Transcription Initiation, Elongation and Termination

levels.kid:
Imagine a train that reads a track and builds a copy as it goes. In your cells, that train is called **RNA polymerase**. The track is a gene in your DNA.

First, the train has to find the right starting station. Then it pulls the two DNA strands apart a little, like unzipping a jacket. That is the start.

Next, the train rolls along the gene. It adds RNA letters one by one, matching each DNA letter. This middle part is the longest.

Finally, the train reaches a stop sign. It lets go of the DNA and the new RNA floats away. Start, go, stop: that is how a cell copies a gene into a message.
levels.hs:
**Transcription** is the copying of a gene's DNA into RNA by the enzyme **RNA polymerase**. It happens in three stages.

- **Initiation**: RNA polymerase binds a DNA region called the **promoter**, just before the gene. It unwinds about 12 to 14 base pairs to form a **transcription bubble**, then begins joining the first RNA nucleotides. It needs no primer, unlike the enzyme that copies DNA.
- **Elongation**: the polymerase moves along the **template strand**, reading it from 3' to 5' and building RNA from 5' to 3'. It adds nucleotides that pair with the template (A pairs with U in RNA, G with C). Behind it, the DNA zips back together.
- **Termination**: at the end of the gene, signals in the DNA or RNA make the polymerase stop and release the RNA.

The RNA matches the other DNA strand, called the **coding strand**, except that it has U where the DNA has T.

A real example: in the bacterium *E. coli*, many genes end with a stretch rich in G and C followed by a run of A's. The RNA copied from it folds into a tight **hairpin** followed by a run of U's. The hairpin jams the polymerase, and the weak A-U pairs let the RNA slip off. This is called **intrinsic termination**.
levels.college:
**Initiation.** In bacteria, the core enzyme (α2ββ'ω) joins a **sigma factor** (σ70 for housekeeping genes) to form the holoenzyme. Sigma recognizes the -35 and -10 promoter elements. The **closed complex** isomerizes into an **open complex** in which roughly 13 bp around the start site (+1) are melted. Initiation is inefficient. During **abortive initiation** the enzyme makes and releases many short transcripts (under about 10 nt) while staying put. It pulls downstream DNA into itself (**scrunching**), and the strain this builds up helps it break free in **promoter escape**. Sigma's contacts are then lost, and sigma is often released. In eukaryotes, Pol II escape follows assembly of the preinitiation complex. **TFIIH** helicase activity opens the DNA, and its kinase (CDK7) phosphorylates **Ser5** of the Pol II CTD heptad repeat (YSPTSPS).

**Elongation.** The polymerase adds NTPs to the RNA 3'-OH. The catalytic center uses two Mg2+ ions and releases pyrophosphate (PPi), which is hydrolysed, making each step favourable. An RNA-DNA hybrid of about 8 to 9 bp sits inside the enzyme. Rates are around 20 to 90 nt/s.
- **Pausing and backtracking**: the polymerase can slide backward, pushing the RNA 3' end out of the active site.
- **Proofreading**: GreA/GreB (bacteria) or **TFIIS** (eukaryotes) stimulate cleavage of the backtracked RNA, so synthesis can resume and misincorporations are removed.
- In eukaryotes, Pol II must push through nucleosomes, helped by **FACT** and histone chaperones.

**Termination.**
- **Intrinsic (Rho-independent)**: a GC-rich hairpin followed by about 7 to 8 U's destabilizes the weak rU:dA hybrid.
- **Rho-dependent**: Rho, a hexameric 5'→3' RNA helicase, loads onto C-rich, unstructured *rut* sites. It translocates along the RNA and pulls it from the paused polymerase.
- **Eukaryotic Pol II**: termination is coupled to 3'-end cleavage at the poly(A) signal. Pol I and Pol III use distinct signals; Pol III stops at runs of T's.
levels.phd:
Single-molecule and structural work reframed initiation as a series of conformational checkpoints. Magnetic-tweezers and FRET experiments (Ebright, Kapanidis and colleagues, 2006) showed that bacterial RNAP does not move during abortive cycling. Instead it **scrunches** downstream DNA into the active-site cleft. The stored stress drives escape once the RNA reaches about 10 to 15 nt and clashes with the sigma region 3.2 linker, which occupies the RNA exit channel. This explains why promoter sequences that strengthen sigma binding can slow escape: very tight binding is not optimal for output.

Elongation is best modelled as a **Brownian ratchet**. RNAP oscillates between pre- and post-translocated states, and NTP binding plus **trigger loop** folding biases it forward. The trigger loop closes over a correctly paired NTP, positioning the two catalytic Mg2+ ions. Its mobility accounts for much of selectivity (error rate roughly 10^-5 to 10^-6 per nucleotide). A **bridge helix** links the conformational changes to translocation. Pauses arise when the enzyme enters an elemental, catalytically inactive state. This can be extended by RNA hairpins in the exit channel (the *his* pause) or by backtracking.

Pol II's CTD acts as a phosphorylation code. Ser5-P (CDK7) marks early elongation and recruits the capping enzyme. Ser2-P accumulates toward 3' ends via **P-TEFb** (CDK9) and CDK12. In metazoans, Pol II stalls 20 to 60 nt downstream of the start site in **promoter-proximal pausing**. Pausing is enforced by DSIF and NELF and released when P-TEFb phosphorylates NELF, DSIF and Ser2. Lis and colleagues' heat-shock work in *Drosophila* established pausing as a regulated step. Global run-on sequencing (GRO-seq) later showed it at most active genes.

Pol II termination has two models that are now seen as unified:
- **Allosteric model**: passing the poly(A) signal changes the conformation of the elongation complex.
- **Torpedo model**: after CPSF73 cleavage, the 5'→3' exonuclease **XRN2** degrades the downstream RNA and dislodges Pol II.

Recent structures suggest that dephosphorylation of SPT5 by PP1 slows Pol II after the poly(A) signal, making it catchable by XRN2. Rho, in turn, is now thought to bind RNAP early ('hitchhiking' models), not only chase it.
levels.expert:
Transcription mechanics are drug targets and disease mechanisms. **Rifampicin** binds the bacterial RNAP β subunit (rpoB) in the RNA exit channel. It does not block initial bond formation; it sterically blocks extension past 2 to 3 nt, trapping abortive initiation. Over 95% of rifampicin-resistant *M. tuberculosis* isolates carry mutations in an 81-bp 'rifampicin resistance-determining region' of rpoB. The GeneXpert MTB/RIF assay detects these mutations within hours, a rare case where a molecular mechanism directly drives a diagnostic. **Fidaxomicin** binds the RNAP 'switch region' and prevents open-complex formation. It is used against *C. difficile* because it largely spares gut commensals. **Bicyclomycin** inhibits Rho and is a research tool for mapping Rho-dependent termination.

In eukaryotes, **α-amanitin** (from *Amanita phalloides*) binds Pol II near the bridge helix and trigger loop and halts translocation. This causes the delayed liver failure of death-cap poisoning, because hepatocytes take up the toxin via OATP1B3. Antibody-drug conjugates now use amanitin payloads against tumours. **Flavopiridol** and selective CDK9 inhibitors block pause release. **THZ1** and related CDK7 inhibitors target transcription-addicted cancers driven by MYC or super-enhancers. The therapeutic index remains the challenge.

For neuroscience, transcriptional kinetics matter. Neuronal **immediate early genes** (Fos, Arc, Npas4) carry paused Pol II, which lets activity-dependent expression begin within minutes. Very long neuronal genes (over 1 Mb, such as some autism-linked genes) take hours to transcribe. They are vulnerable to topoisomerase inhibition, as shown by King, Zylka and colleagues (2013). Hexanucleotide repeat expansions in **C9orf72** (ALS/FTD) produce abortive and repeat-containing transcripts. Elongation factor SPT4 has been explored as a target to reduce them.

Methodological pitfalls: ChIP-seq Pol II peaks conflate paused and slowly elongating enzyme. Nascent methods give strand- and nucleotide-resolution views: PRO-seq, NET-seq, and TT-seq for synthesis rates. Open questions include how the speed of elongation influences co-transcriptional splicing choices. Another is how Pol II resolves collisions with replication forks, a source of genome instability.

keyPoints: Transcription has three stages: initiation, elongation and termination
RNA polymerase needs no primer and builds RNA 5' to 3' from the template strand
Abortive initiation and DNA scrunching precede promoter escape
TFIIS and GreA/B rescue backtracked polymerase and aid proofreading
Bacteria terminate by GC hairpin plus U-run (intrinsic) or by the Rho helicase
Pol II CTD phosphorylation (Ser5 then Ser2) and XRN2 torpedo coordinate eukaryotic transcription

lessons.title: The 5' Cap and the Poly(A) Tail

levels.kid:
When a cell copies a gene, it makes a message called **mRNA**. But a bare message is fragile. Little cutting machines in the cell would chew it up fast.

So the cell adds two special pieces. At the front end it puts a **cap**, like a hat. The cap protects the front and tells the cell's protein builders, "Start reading here!"

At the back end it adds a long **tail** made of many copies of one letter, A. The tail is like the long string on a kite. It keeps the message safe, and it slowly gets shorter over time. When the tail gets too short, the message is cleaned away.

Cap on the front, tail on the back: now the message is ready to leave the nucleus and do its job.
levels.hs:
In eukaryotic cells, a newly made RNA copy of a gene (the **pre-mRNA**) gets modified before it becomes mature **messenger RNA (mRNA)**. Two of the most important changes happen at its ends.

- **The 5' cap**: right after RNA polymerase II starts copying a gene, enzymes attach a modified guanine nucleotide, **7-methylguanosine (m7G)**, to the front (5') end. It is joined in an unusual backward way, through a **5'-to-5' triphosphate bridge**.
- **The poly(A) tail**: at the back (3') end, the RNA is cut at a specific spot and an enzyme adds a long string of adenine nucleotides, often about 200-250 in mammals.

Why bother? These ends do several jobs:
- **Protection**: enzymes called **exonucleases** chew RNA from the ends. The cap and tail block them.
- **Export**: they help move the mRNA out of the nucleus.
- **Translation**: ribosomes use the cap to find the start of the message, and the tail helps them work efficiently.
- **Lifespan**: the tail slowly shortens in the cytoplasm, acting like a timer. When it gets short, the mRNA is destroyed.

A real example: the COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were built with a 5' cap and a poly(A) tail, because without them the vaccine mRNA would be degraded quickly and poorly translated. Bacterial mRNAs, by contrast, have no m7G cap.
levels.college:
Both ends of a eukaryotic pre-mRNA are processed **co-transcriptionally**, coordinated by the **C-terminal domain (CTD)** of RNA polymerase II, a tail of heptad repeats (YSPTSPS) whose phosphorylation pattern recruits processing enzymes at the right time.

**Capping** (after roughly 20-30 nucleotides, recruited by Ser5-phosphorylated CTD):
- **RNA triphosphatase** removes the terminal (gamma) phosphate from the 5' triphosphate.
- **Guanylyltransferase** adds GMP (from GTP), forming a 5'-5' triphosphate linkage.
- **Guanine-N7 methyltransferase** methylates the guanine, using S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) as the methyl donor, giving the **cap 0** structure (m7GpppN).
- In mammals the first transcribed nucleotides are often 2'-O-methylated (**cap 1**, **cap 2**).

In the nucleus the cap is bound by the **cap-binding complex (CBC: CBP80/CBP20)**, which aids splicing of the first intron and export. In the cytoplasm it is swapped for **eIF4E**, part of eIF4F, which recruits the small ribosomal subunit.

**3' end formation** (linked to Ser2-phosphorylated CTD):
- **CPSF** recognizes the **AAUAAA** signal; **CstF** binds a GU/U-rich element downstream.
- Cleavage occurs about 10-30 nt downstream of AAUAAA, catalyzed by **CPSF73**.
- **Poly(A) polymerase (PAP)** adds adenosines template-free; **PABPN1** speeds synthesis and helps set length.

In the cytoplasm, **PABPC** coats the tail and binds **eIF4G**, which also binds eIF4E. This forms the **closed-loop** model, linking cap and tail to boost translation.

**Exceptions**: replication-dependent histone mRNAs lack poly(A) tails and end in a stem-loop bound by SLBP; mitochondrial and bacterial mRNAs lack m7G caps.
levels.phd:
**Capping chemistry and quality control.** Metazoans use a bifunctional capping enzyme (RNGTT) with triphosphatase and guanylyltransferase domains; RNMT (with activator RAMAC) then N7-methylates. CMTR1 and CMTR2 produce cap 1 and cap 2 via ribose 2'-O-methylation, and if the first nucleotide is adenosine, PCIF1 can N6-methylate it (m6Am). Capping is a checkpoint: DXO/DXO-family enzymes and the DcpS scavenger remove incomplete or aberrant caps. Some RNAs carry non-canonical NAD+ caps, incorporated at initiation in place of ATP.

**Cap 1 as self-marker.** The 2'-O-methyl distinguishes self from non-self RNA. The innate sensor IFIT1 binds cap 0 RNAs, and RIG-I discriminates against cap 1, which explains why many viruses encode their own 2'-O-methyltransferases or "cap-snatch" (influenza polymerase steals capped host fragments).

**Polyadenylation machinery.** CPSF subunits CPSF30 and WDR33 directly read AAUAAA (AUUAAA is the main variant); CPSF73 is the endonuclease, built around a metallo-beta-lactamase fold. CFIm (binding UGUA upstream) and CFIIm also contribute, and symplekin scaffolds the complex. Tail length is roughly 200-250 nt in mammals and about 70-90 in yeast, set by PABPN1 and PAP processivity.

**Termination coupling.** Cleavage generates an uncapped 5' end on the downstream RNA, which the 5'-3' exonuclease XRN2 degrades. In the "torpedo" model this chases down and helps release Pol II; the allosteric model proposes conformational change after passing the poly(A) signal. Current evidence supports a unified hybrid.

**Alternative polyadenylation (APA).** Over half of human genes have multiple poly(A) sites. Choosing proximal sites shortens 3' UTRs, removing miRNA and ARE binding sites. Proliferating and cancer cells favor shorter 3' UTRs (Sandberg et al., 2008; Mayr and Bartel, 2009), whereas neurons extend them markedly.

**Controversy on the closed loop.** Single-molecule and global studies show tail length correlates poorly with translation in steady-state somatic cells, though it strongly matters in oocytes and early embryos (Subtelny et al., 2014).
levels.expert:
**Engineering ends for RNA therapeutics.** Synthetic mRNA design turns on capping. Early anti-reverse cap analogs (ARCA) prevented backward incorporation but gave cap 0 at modest efficiency. Co-transcriptional trinucleotide analogs such as CleanCap AG produce cap 1 directly in high yield and are used in the Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna COVID-19 vaccines. Poly(A) tails are encoded in the DNA template; BNT162b2 uses a segmented tail (30 A, a linker, then 70 A) to reduce plasmid instability in E. coli. Residual uncapped 5'-triphosphate RNA and double-stranded byproducts trigger RIG-I and MDA5, so purification and N1-methylpseudouridine substitution matter alongside cap 1.

**Measuring tails.** Tail length was historically hard to read by sequencing because homopolymers confuse polymerases. PAL-seq and TAIL-seq, and now direct nanopore RNA sequencing and FLAM-seq, measure tails genome-wide and revealed non-A residues (guanylation by TENT4A/B shields tails from deadenylation; HBV and HCMV hijack this).

**Deadenylation as the decay trigger.** CCR4-NOT and PAN2-PAN3 shorten tails; below about 10-20 nt, LSM1-7/PATL1 bind and promote decapping by DCP2, followed by XRN1 5'-3' decay. miRNA silencing works largely by recruiting CCR4-NOT via GW182/TNRC6.

**Disease and drug links.**
- A G-to-A mutation (20210) in the prothrombin 3' end enhances cleavage efficiency, raising thrombosis risk.
- In oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy, a GCN repeat expansion lengthens PABPN1's polyalanine stretch, causing nuclear aggregates.
- APA shifts in cancer can release oncogenes such as CCND1 from miRNA repression.
- Cordycepin (3'-deoxyadenosine) terminates poly(A) addition and is a research tool.
- eIF4E is overexpressed in many tumors; cap-competitive inhibitors and antisense approaches have been explored, with limited clinical success.

**Neuroscience angle.** Local translation in dendrites relies on cytoplasmic polyadenylation (CPEB with GLD2), linking tail extension to synaptic plasticity and memory consolidation.

**Open questions**: how APA choice is coordinated with chromatin and Pol II speed, and when tail length actually limits translation in adult tissues.

keyPoints: Eukaryotic mRNA gets an m7G cap at the 5' end via a 5'-5' triphosphate bridge
Capping uses triphosphatase, guanylyltransferase and N7-methyltransferase, early in transcription
CPSF reads AAUAAA; cleavage is followed by template-free poly(A) addition by poly(A) polymerase
Cap and tail protect from exonucleases and aid export and translation (eIF4E-PABP closed loop)
Tail shortening (deadenylation) times mRNA decay; cap 1 marks RNA as self to innate immunity
Alternative polyadenylation changes 3' UTR length and regulation; mRNA vaccines use engineered caps and tails

lessons.title: Splicing and the Spliceosome

levels.kid:
Imagine a recipe card with extra nonsense words mixed in. Before you cook, you cut out the nonsense parts and tape the good parts back together. Your cells do the same thing with their messages!

When a cell copies a gene, the copy is made of **RNA**. It has useful pieces called **exons** and in-between pieces called **introns**. The introns must be cut out.

A tiny machine called the **spliceosome** does the cutting. It finds the edges of each intron, snips it out, and joins the exons together neatly.

Here is a cool trick. By keeping different exons, a cell can make different messages from one gene. That is like making pancakes or waffles from the same batter!
levels.hs:
In eukaryotes like humans, genes are usually split. The coding parts, called **exons**, are separated by non-coding stretches called **introns**. RNA polymerase copies the whole gene, introns included, into a **pre-mRNA**. Before the message can be translated, the introns must be removed and the exons joined. This is **splicing**.

Splicing is done by the **spliceosome**, a large machine built from five small RNAs (called **snRNAs**: U1, U2, U4, U5 and U6) plus well over a hundred proteins. The snRNAs pair with short signals in the intron:
- the **5' splice site**, which usually starts the intron with GU
- the **branch point**, an A nucleotide near the end of the intron
- the **3' splice site**, which usually ends the intron with AG

The intron is released as a loop shaped like a cowboy's rope, called a **lariat**.

Splicing also allows **alternative splicing**: including or skipping different exons to make several proteins from one gene. Over 90% of human multi-exon genes are alternatively spliced. One example is the fruit fly *Dscam* gene. It can, in theory, produce over 38,000 versions, which helps its neurons tell themselves apart.

Mistakes matter. About 10-15% or more of disease-causing mutations disrupt splicing.
levels.college:
Splicing removes introns through two sequential **transesterification reactions**. No net bonds are gained or lost, so the chemistry itself needs no ATP. ATP is used by the spliceosome's helicases to rearrange RNA.

**Splice signals (major, U2-type introns):**
- 5' splice site: exon|**GU**RAGU
- Branch point: a conserved **adenosine**, usually 18-40 nt upstream of the 3' site
- **Polypyrimidine tract** (C/U-rich), then the 3' splice site: **AG**|exon

**The two steps:**
1. The 2'-OH of the branch-point A attacks the 5' splice site. This frees exon 1 and forms a **2'-5' phosphodiester** bond, creating the lariat intermediate.
2. The freed 3'-OH of exon 1 attacks the 3' splice site. The exons are joined and the lariat intron is released.

**Spliceosome assembly** is stepwise and dynamic:
- **E complex**: U1 snRNP base-pairs with the 5' site. **SF1** binds the branch point, and **U2AF** (U2AF65 and U2AF35) binds the polypyrimidine tract and the AG.
- **A complex**: U2 snRNP pairs with the branch region and bulges out the branch A.
- **B complex**: the U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP joins.
- **Activation**: U1 and U4 leave. U6 takes over pairing at the 5' site and pairs with U2, forming the catalytic core (B act, then C).

**Alternative splicing** is regulated by cis elements: exonic and intronic splicing **enhancers** and **silencers**. Trans factors read these elements. **SR proteins** usually promote exon inclusion, and **hnRNPs** often repress it. Common patterns include:
- cassette exon skipping
- mutually exclusive exons
- alternative 5' or 3' sites
- intron retention

Splicing is largely **co-transcriptional**. The RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain (CTD) recruits splicing factors, linking this step to capping and polyadenylation.
levels.phd:
The spliceosome is a **ribozyme**. Cryo-EM structures from the Shi, Nagai and Lührmann labs (2015 onward) showed that the U6 snRNA ISL and the U2/U6 helices position two catalytic Mg2+ ions. These ions are coordinated by U6 phosphates in a geometry resembling **group II self-splicing introns**, supporting a shared evolutionary origin. **Prp8**, the largest and most conserved protein, forms a scaffold around this RNA active site but does not itself catalyse the reaction.

The conformational cycle is driven by eight conserved DExD/H-box ATPases:
- **Prp5** and **Sub2/UAP56** act early.
- **Prp28** transfers the 5' site from U1 to the U6 ACAGAGA box.
- **Brr2** unwinds U4/U6 for activation.
- **Prp2** remodels B act to B*.
- **Prp16** drives the switch from the step 1 to the step 2 conformation.
- **Prp22** releases the mRNA.
- **Prp43** disassembles the intron lariat spliceosome.

Proofreading uses kinetic competition. Prp16 and Prp22 reject suboptimal substrates by acting before slow chemistry can occur.

A **minor (U12-type) spliceosome** removes about 0.5% of human introns, roughly 700-800. It uses U11, U12, U4atac and U6atac with the shared U5, and recognises distinct, highly conserved 5' sites and branch points.

Intron definition, used in yeast with short introns, contrasts with **exon definition** in vertebrates. In vertebrates, long introns force U1 and U2AF to pair across the short exon first, and later the cross-intron interactions form. This explains why many vertebrate splice-site mutations cause exon skipping.

Regulation is combinatorial and depends on position. RNA maps from CLIP studies show that NOVA, RBFOX and PTBP1 activate exons when bound downstream but repress them when bound upstream. **Kinetic coupling** adds another layer: slower Pol II elongation favours inclusion of weak exons (Kornblihtt). Splicing also deposits the **exon junction complex** about 20-24 nt upstream of each junction. This feeds into mRNA export and nonsense-mediated decay.

A live controversy is how much alternative splicing yields functional proteins. Transcriptomics detects vast isoform diversity, but proteomics recovers far fewer isoforms. Many isoforms may be noise or targets of NMD.
levels.expert:
Clinically, splicing is both a disease mechanism and a drug target, which matters directly for a future neurosurgeon.

**Variant interpretation.** Standard pipelines under-call splicing variants. Deep-intronic changes can create cryptic exons, called pseudoexons. A classic example is the CEP290 c.2991+1655A>G variant in Leber congenital amaurosis. Synonymous "silent" changes can also disrupt exonic enhancers. Deep-learning predictors such as **SpliceAI** (Jaganathan et al., 2019) estimated that about 9-11% of pathogenic de novo variants in neurodevelopmental disorders act via cryptic splicing. Functional confirmation by RNA-seq from blood or fibroblasts, or by minigene assays, is increasingly expected. A key pitfall is that clinically accessible tissues may not express brain-specific isoforms.

**Splicing therapeutics.**
- **Nusinersen** is a 2'-MOE antisense oligonucleotide given intrathecally. It blocks the ISS-N1 silencer in SMN2 intron 7, restoring exon 7 inclusion in spinal muscular atrophy.
- **Risdiplam** is an oral small molecule that stabilises the U1 snRNP interaction at the SMN2 exon 7 5' site. It is a landmark proof that RNA-protein interfaces are druggable.
- **Eteplirsen** and related drugs induce exon skipping in DMD to restore the reading frame. However, their clinical benefit remains debated because the dystrophin increases are modest.
- **Milasen** (2019) was a custom ASO for a single child with Batten disease. It masked a retrotransposon-created cryptic splice site and raised regulatory questions about N-of-1 therapies.

**Cancer and neuro-oncology.** Recurrent mutations in **SF3B1**, **U2AF1**, **SRSF2** and **ZRSR2** occur in myelodysplastic syndromes and CLL. SF3B1 hotspots such as K700E shift branch-point selection and activate cryptic 3' sites. Spliceosome-targeting compounds like H3B-8800 showed limited efficacy. Gliomas show widespread mis-splicing, including the PTBP1-driven PKM2 isoform switch and the oncogenic EGFRvIII deletion variant.

**Neurodegeneration.** When **TDP-43** is lost from the nucleus in ALS/FTD, cryptic exons appear in **STMN2** and **UNC13A**. These are now candidate biomarkers and ASO targets.

**Open questions.** Researchers still need to learn how to target splicing in specific cells, how to deliver therapies beyond the CNS and liver, and which isoforms are truly functional and which are noise.

keyPoints: Splicing removes introns from pre-mRNA and joins exons
The spliceosome uses five snRNAs (U1, U2, U4, U5, U6) plus many proteins
Intron signals: GU at the 5' end, a branch-point A, and AG at the 3' end
Two transesterifications release the intron as a lariat
Alternative splicing makes several proteins from one gene
Splicing defects cause disease and are targets of drugs like nusinersen

test.q: Which parts of a pre-mRNA are removed during splicing?
test.explain: Introns are the non-coding stretches cut out. Exons are kept and joined together.

test.q: Which dinucleotide usually begins a major-class intron at its 5' end?
test.explain: Most introns start with GU and end with AG (the GU-AG rule). AG marks the 3' end, not the start.

test.q: What shape does the excised intron take?
test.explain: The branch-point A forms a 2'-5' bond with the intron's 5' end, creating a loop with a tail called a lariat.

test.q: Which nucleotide at the branch point attacks the 5' splice site?
test.explain: The 2'-OH of a conserved branch-point adenosine performs the first transesterification.

test.q: Which snRNP first base-pairs with the 5' splice site?
test.explain: U1 recognises the 5' site in the E complex. U6 later replaces it during activation.

test.q: Why does the splicing chemistry itself need no ATP?
choices: Mg2+ ions supply energy for bond formation
Phosphodiester bonds are exchanged, not newly made
The spliceosome uses GTP for each cut instead
Introns carry stored energy from transcription
test.explain: Transesterifications swap one phosphodiester bond for another. ATP powers the helicases that remodel the spliceosome.

test.q: SR proteins binding exonic splicing enhancers typically:
test.explain: SR proteins usually promote inclusion. hnRNPs often repress it.

test.q: The fruit fly Dscam gene illustrates:
test.explain: Dscam can theoretically produce over 38,000 isoforms through mutually exclusive exons.

test.q: Which factor binds the polypyrimidine tract near the 3' splice site?
test.explain: U2AF65 binds the pyrimidine tract, and U2AF35 binds the AG in the early E complex.

test.q: What is the large RNA-protein machine that removes introns called?
test.explain: The spliceosome is built from five snRNPs plus many proteins.

test.q: Making several proteins from one gene by choosing different exons is called ___ splicing.
test.explain: Over 90% of human multi-exon genes undergo alternative splicing.

test.q: What is the abbreviation for the small nuclear RNAs in the spliceosome?
test.explain: snRNAs (in snRNP particles) such as U1 and U2 pair with intron signals.

kidTest.q: What does the spliceosome do?
choices: Cuts out extra pieces of RNA
kidTest.explain: It removes introns and joins the useful pieces.

kidTest.q: What are the useful pieces that are kept called?
kidTest.explain: Exons are kept and joined together.

kidTest.q: What happens to the introns?
kidTest.explain: Introns are snipped out of the message.

kidTest.q: Why is keeping different exons useful?
choices: It makes many messages from one gene
It makes the whole cell grow bigger
It helps the cell divide much faster
kidTest.explain: Like pancakes or waffles from one batter!

kidTest.q: Cells copy genes into a message made of this. Hint: R _ _
kidTest.explain: The gene copy is made of RNA.

advancedTest.q: A vertebrate 5' splice-site mutation most often causes exon skipping rather than intron retention because:
choices: U6 snRNA is absent from vertebrate catalytic cores
Splice sites are first paired across the short exon
Vertebrate introns are too short to be retained
advancedTest.explain: Under exon definition, U1 and U2AF pair across the exon first. Losing one site disrupts recognition of the whole exon, so it is skipped.

advancedTest.q: Which observation best supports a shared origin of the spliceosome and group II introns?
choices: Both depend on ATP to make phosphodiester bonds
Both splice introns ending in a GU dinucleotide
Both are built mainly around the Prp8 protein
Their catalytic RNA positions two Mg2+ ions alike
advancedTest.explain: Cryo-EM showed U6 RNA coordinating two metal ions in a geometry resembling group II ribozymes. Prp8 is a scaffold and is not found in group II introns.

advancedTest.q: Slowing RNA polymerase II elongation tends to increase inclusion of a weak exon because:
choices: The minor spliceosome takes over at slower rates
Slow elongation blocks hnRNPs from binding the RNA
The weak exon gets time to assemble before rivals form
Slow Pol II adds more SR proteins to the CTD
advancedTest.explain: Kinetic coupling gives a weak upstream exon a window to be recognised before a stronger downstream site is transcribed and competes.

advancedTest.q: Risdiplam is notable mechanistically because it:
choices: Base-pairs with ISS-N1 like an antisense drug
Removes cryptic exons created by TDP-43 loss
Inhibits SF3B1 to slow cancer cell growth
Stabilises U1 binding at an SMN2 5' splice site
advancedTest.explain: Risdiplam is a small molecule that strengthens the U1 snRNP interaction at the exon 7 5' site. Base-pairing with ISS-N1 describes nusinersen, an antisense oligonucleotide.
